archetype.name: Dual-Threat (power runner near the goal line)
archetype.definition: A big-armed passer who wins through the air at every depth, scrambles to bail out broken plays, and serves as his offense's short-yardage and goal-line runner.

report.headline: Career-best yards per attempt, a deep game that pays, and unsustainable goal-line touchdowns
report.take:
Allen is playing the most efficient downfield football of his career. His 8.8 yards per attempt ranks 3rd of 45 qualifiers and beats every full season he has had, including last year's 7.97. His 0.29 EPA per dropback ranks 6th. This is not dink-and-dunk efficiency. His aggressiveness is up 1.6 points from last year, and the passes of 10-plus air yards have carried the attack at 0.599 EPA per play against 0.266 underneath. Keon Coleman has become the vertical outlet: 0.959 EPA per target on 25 looks, the most value of any receiver by a wide margin. Volume stays modest at 28.5 attempts a game because Buffalo runs more than the situation calls for (pass rate over expected -3.1, 23rd).

The fantasy number, 26.9 PPR a game and 1st at the position, rests on something that won't keep going: eight rushing touchdowns in six games. Six came on designed runs that average 2.48 yards a carry with a 69.6% success rate. Those are short-yardage plunges, not open-field runs. He really is the Bills' goal-line back, so that role will hold. A per-game touchdown rate like this one won't. The scrambles are the sturdier part of the run game: 17 of them for 1.247 EPA each and 12 first downs.

Two things in the numbers deserve more attention than they get. First, his red-zone passing has been poor: -0.051 EPA, a 48.4% completion rate and -7.4 CPOE inside the 20. The rushing touchdowns hide this, because he finishes drives himself when the throws aren't there. Second, the miss rate has crept up. His bad-throw rate is 14%, 26th of 38 and up two points from last year. LAC (26.9%) and the Rams (27.8%) were two genuinely loose games, and the three deep interceptions come with the territory of how often he lets it fly. The 31.6% pressure-to-sack rate looks ugly. But it is milder than last year's 40.4%, and it is the price of a quarterback who holds the ball (2.97 seconds) to find scrambles and shots. Here the scrambles more than pay for it.

The environment guarantees he keeps throwing with purpose. Buffalo's defense ranks 32nd in EPA, and five of six games have gone over the total. Most of his dropbacks have come in one-score games, where he has been sharp (6.5 CPOE) and better still in close fourth quarters (0.396 EPA). Expect the passing efficiency to hold near its current level, maybe a shade lower. Expect the fantasy line to drift down as the rushing touchdowns slow, which already showed in a 22.4-point average over the last three games.

strengths.title: Vertical passing that offsets its misses
strengths.body: On 26 throws of 20-plus air yards he has averaged 0.823 EPA with four touchdowns, despite completing only 38.5% of them. Coleman's 0.959 EPA per target is the engine. The intermediate range backs it up with a 62.5% success rate and 9.6 CPOE, so this is not one long ball inflating the line. The sample is small, but his arm talent and aggressiveness have been constants for years, so a strong share of it should stick.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for the sacks
strengths.body: He scrambles on 8.4% of dropbacks. Those 17 runs have produced 1.247 EPA apiece and 12 first downs. That is the reason his long time to throw and so-so pressure-to-sack rate don't sink drives. Rushing production has been in the top three of the league in most of his seasons, so this is a durable trait, not a hot streak.

strengths.title: Sharp when the game is close
strengths.body: Nearly all his dropbacks have come within one score. There he posts 6.5 CPOE, and in close fourth quarters he climbs to 0.396 EPA per play. Buffalo's porous defense keeps creating these games, so the high-leverage volume will keep coming.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate built on plunges
concerns.body: Six of his eight rushing touchdowns came on designed runs averaging 2.48 yards a carry. That is a goal-line role, not an explosive one. He will keep getting those chances, but scoring this often on so few carries regresses hard. It is the biggest reason his fantasy output should come down from its 1st-ranked level.

concerns.title: Red-zone passing has stalled
concerns.body: Inside the 20 he completes 48.4% with -7.4 CPOE and negative EPA, even with five touchdown passes. When the field shrinks, his rushing has masked a passing game that isn't finishing drives. If the short-yardage runs dry up, this is where drives will stall.

concerns.title: Loose throws and turnover risk
concerns.body: His bad-throw rate of 14% is up two points on last year, and his interception rate ranks 32nd of 45. He also has four turnover-worthy fumbles. Part of this is the cost of throwing deep: three of the four picks came on 20-plus throws. Still, he has a long career history of double-digit interception seasons, so it is part of who he is rather than a blip.

trend.note: His passing has been consistent: 0.268 EPA per dropback over the last three games against 0.29 for the season, and a lower sack rate lately. The volatility is in the fantasy line, which has swung with rushing touchdowns and one 121-yard rushing game. His last three games averaged 22.4 PPR after 40.8 back in Week 2.

nextGame.headline: Ravens' leaky deep defense, missing safety, meet Allen's best throws
nextGame.body:
Baltimore's defense is middling overall (20th in EPA), but its shape suits Allen. It ranks 6th against short passes and 26th against deep ones (0.842 EPA allowed). That pushes him toward exactly the throws that have driven his season. Opposing WR1s have feasted, at 0.77 EPA per play (32nd). Tight ends have been held down (5th), which points targets toward Coleman and Shakir and away from Kincaid. The Ravens hit quarterbacks often (6th in hit rate), so expect some pressure. His scrambles are the counter. Buffalo comes off a bye with 14 days of rest, is a 3.5-point home favorite, and the total is a lofty 53.5.

Availability tilts his way. Safety Jaylinn Hawkins (81% of snaps) is out, and linebacker Tavius Robinson (72%) is on IR. Both thin the coverage behind a defense that already leaks deep. Lamar Jackson is listed out with an ankle sprain, but the Ravens' coach says he is in a decent spot to play. If he goes, Baltimore's 8th-ranked offense against Buffalo's 32nd-ranked defense sets up another shootout that keeps Allen throwing. DJ Moore (questionable, shoulder, 53% of snaps) is the only Buffalo issue. Losing him trims a secondary option more than the core of the passing game.

keyMatchups.title: Allen's deep game vs a leaky secondary
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore allows 0.842 EPA on deep passes, 26th in the league. Allen produces 0.823 EPA on his own deep throws. With Hawkins out, the back end loses a regular starter. This is the matchup most likely to decide his day.

keyMatchups.title: Short game runs into resistance
keyMatchups.body: The Ravens are 6th against short passes, and tight ends have produced -0.07 EPA per play against them. Kincaid's usual underneath volume may be less efficient than usual, so expect Allen to need the intermediate and deep levels to move the ball.

keyMatchups.title: Lamar's status sets the script
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo's defense ranks last in EPA. If Jackson plays, Baltimore's offense can force the Bills to keep throwing in close-game states, where Allen has been at his best. If Jackson sits, a more comfortable lead could tilt Buffalo toward its run-leaning default.

nextGame.watch: How often Allen gets Coleman isolated deep against a Ravens secondary missing its starting safety.

restOfSeason.body:
Allen's passing looks real. A strong CPOE, high-end depth production and a career trend of top-10 efficiency all support it, though 8.8 yards per attempt will probably settle slightly lower as the deep completions even out. Buffalo's last-ranked defense should keep him in competitive, pass-friendly game states, while the run-leaning play-calling holds attempts in the high 20s. I'd expect roughly 235-270 passing yards and 1.3-1.9 touchdown passes a game.

The rushing touchdowns are where the regression lands. He will stay the goal-line and short-yardage option, so 0.4-0.7 rushing scores a game is a fair band, well below what he has done so far. Scrambles should keep rushing yards around 30-45. That brings him to about 21-26 PPR a game: still near the top of the position, but not the current pace.
swingFactors: How long the short-yardage rushing touchdowns keep coming
Whether Buffalo's defense keeps forcing shootouts
Health of the receiver group, Coleman and Moore especially

confidence.note: Six games; passing traits match his career, but the rushing-TD output rests on a small, volatile sample.
